cells.tense: You are here now, and the room between you and other people is steady.
cells.ask: In one conversation today, stay with what someone feels without taking it on as yours. Afterwards, notice that you stayed.
cells.core:
You can sit near someone's fear or grief and stay yourself. You don't have to fix it and you don't have to match it. The space between you stays open, and that's what lets the other person feel what they feel without meeting a wall or a rescue.

It isn't something you push into place. It happens in a moment and you don't name it. What this balance is free to feed next is steadiness — the kind of weight-bearing that makes a room worth staying in. You can be the one who stays calm and still know where you end and they begin.
cells.sheetLine: You stay with people's feelings and stay yourself too.
cells.verb: tending the space between people so feeling can move without anyone drowning
cells.place: the moment before any of it is chosen or named, where everything is still possible

cells.tense: You are already braced for how this will go, ahead of it happening.
cells.ask: Let one person's feeling be theirs today. Don't move to fix it or steer it. Watch what happens when you don't.
cells.core:
Staying close to someone's feeling is the thing that works here. You can be near it, name it, keep it from tipping over. The trouble starts when that closeness turns into planning — arranging what someone might need and how to keep it steady, before anything has happened. Being near feelings has become managing them.

What sits underneath is care, and that part is fine. What's needed is to let one thing run its course and not save it. If a feeling finishes and nothing breaks, you'll have something real to trust. The grip can loosen, and the person stays.

cells.tense: You are with people, and some part of you is standing just outside the room.
cells.ask: Say one thing you actually feel, out loud, to one person this week. Keep it short. Let it be heard without explaining it.
cells.core:
You're often the one keeping things calm, and you do it well — but no one can tell where you are in it, including you. You're present and not arriving. Standing back keeps the temperature even and keeps you out of the picture.

Warmth isn't the problem. The part where you're a person in the room has gone quiet, and it fills back slowly. Don't push feeling into that quiet. Get clear on what's yours versus what you picked up from whoever you're with. One small true thing, said and left alone, starts to put you back on the ground you're already standing on.

cells.tense: You are already steadying the room between people, and calling it something smaller.
cells.ask: Notice one moment today when you steady someone without planning to. Say to yourself: that was mine.
cells.core:
You're already tending the space between people. It's in how you listen, what you don't say, the way you keep a conversation from tipping. It runs in you — you just don't claim it. Asked about it, you'd probably say you're easygoing, or you just try to keep things calm, or that's how you are.

That's not the whole of it. There's real skill here, and the one person who gets no credit for it is the one doing it. Nothing about what you do needs to change. What's missing is saying so — to yourself first, maybe out loud later. It gets steadier when you know it's yours.
